one_liner: Single-header, in-situ C++11 JSON DOM parser; 1.1-1.8x faster than RapidJSON insitu in the simdjson paper.
what_it_does: sajson parses a complete UTF-8 JSON buffer in place into one contiguous AST of machine words. It returns a move-only sajson::document whose sajson::value views give O(1) array indexing and key lookup by linear scan, switching to binary search once an object has more than 100 keys. It is not a RapidJSON drop-in: the API is read-only (no writer, no DOM mutation, no SAX), the allocation strategy (single_allocation, dynamic_allocation, bounded_allocation) is chosen per call, and errors come back through document::is_valid() with line, column and message instead of exceptions. Pass mutable_string_view(len, ptr) to parse your own buffer in place; passing sajson::string or literal makes a heap copy first.
how_it_is_fast: In single-allocation mode one buffer of one word per input byte holds both the parse stack, which grows up from the bottom, and the AST, which is written down from the top, so the hot path has no capacity checks. Values are tagged words with 3 low tag bits, and null/true/false take no storage. The parser is a goto-based state machine with an explicit stack (no recursion) and __builtin_expect branch hints. It scans strings 4 bytes per iteration through a 256-entry lookup table and drops to a slow path only for escapes or non-ASCII bytes. Strings are unescaped and NUL-terminated inside the input buffer, so no string copies are made. There is no SIMD, and numbers use a plain digit loop scaled by a power-of-10 table.
when_to_use: Read-only, single-pass parsing of complete UTF-8 documents already in a writable buffer (file read, network receive buffer) where the buffer can outlive the parsed document.
String- and object-heavy payloads such as API responses and logs: the paper's gains over RapidJSON insitu include apache_builds 1.2 vs 0.80 GB/s and twitter 1.0 vs 0.72 GB/s.

Embedded, mobile or WebAssembly builds that need zero library allocations: bounded_allocation parses into a caller-owned size_t array, with no exceptions, RTTI or longjmp, and the README calls the code size suitable for Emscripten.
Code that needs random access into the parsed tree: O(1) array element access and key lookup (binary search above 100 keys), unlike linked-list DOMs.
Deeply nested or adversarial structure where native stack overflow is a concern: parsing uses O(1) C stack and has been fuzzed with AFL.
when_not_to_use: Payloads with 64-bit integers such as IDs: only int32 is stored as an integer, and larger values silently become doubles that lose precision above 2^53 (issue #39, open since 2017).

When strict conformance matters: UTF-8 validation is partial (it accepts overlong forms, encoded surrogates, code points above U+10FFFF and stray continuation-byte leads such as 0xb1 0x87), scalar roots like `42` are rejected (issue #46), and doubles are not always correctly rounded (issue #10; open PR #59 shows 1.65 parsing to the wrong neighbor).
When you must write, modify or stream JSON: there is no serializer, no mutable DOM and no incremental or SAX mode.

Large documents on memory-tight hosts in the fastest mode: single allocation reserves 8 bytes per input byte on 64-bit. Dynamic mode is 10-40% slower per the README, and in the paper it loses to RapidJSON insitu on 6 of 14 files.
Peak throughput or active maintenance: simdjson is 1.4-2.9x faster on the same 14 files, yyjson's README shows 1.80 vs 1.16 GB/s on twitter.json, and sajson's parser code has not changed since 2021.

integration.dependencies: none (C++ standard library only; SAJSON_NO_STD_STRING removes the <string> dependency)
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 per README, and the Bazel library target uses -std=c++11. However, current master defines its lookup table as an in-class constexpr static member with no out-of-class definition. Issue #48 reports undefined-reference link errors from `g++-9 -g` and GCC 10 builds, and the repo's Bazel tests build with -std=c++17. Use C++17 or apply open PR #54.
integration.platforms: any; portable scalar C++ with no SIMD. The SCons matrix builds gcc and clang for 32- and 64-bit; the header has MSVC-specific macros; the repo includes a Swift binding.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The parser keeps no mutable global state (only a constexpr lookup table), so parses of separate buffers are independent. document is move-only and value objects are read-only views into it. mutable_string_view shares copied input through a non-atomic refcount, so do not copy those views across threads.

gotchas: The input buffer is overwritten: escapes are decoded in place and the closing quote becomes NUL. The buffer must stay writable and alive for the document's lifetime, and embedded \u0000 truncates as_cstring() results.

Objects with more than 100 keys are sorted at parse time (by length, then bytes), so get_object_key(i) no longer follows document order unless SAJSON_UNSORTED_OBJECT_KEYS is defined, which makes all lookups linear. Duplicate keys are accepted without error.
Type and bounds checks are assert()-only: calling get_integer_value() on a double or indexing past get_length() is undefined behavior in NDEBUG builds. A missing key returns a null value.
Buffer sizes are in size_t words, not bytes (issue #51). A caller-supplied single_allocation buffer fails with ERROR_OUT_OF_MEMORY unless it has at least one word per input byte.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Over gason, pick sajson when you need indexed access (gason uses linked lists without random access) or parse string- and object-heavy data (paper: apache_builds 1.2 vs 0.91 GB/s, twitter 1.0 vs 0.80), but gason wins number-heavy files (canada 0.95 vs 0.76, mesh 0.77 vs 0.62). simdjson and yyjson are faster; yyjson also reads int64 exactly, and simdjson leaves the input untouched. Choose sajson over them only when a tiny single header with a zero-allocation bounded mode and O(1) indexed DOM access matters more than peak speed.
verified_claims_summary: The peer-reviewed simdjson paper (Skylake i7-6700, GCC 9.1 -O3 -march=native) compared a 2018-09-20 sajson snapshot using a pre-sized bounded buffer against RapidJSON 1.1.0 with UTF-8 validation. sajson parsed all 14 files at 0.62-1.2 GB/s, against 0.41-1.0 GB/s for RapidJSON insitu (1.1-1.8x) and 0.38-0.86 GB/s for RapidJSON default. yyjson's README independently shows twitter.json at 1.16 vs 0.77 GB/s (AMD EPYC 7R32, gcc 9.3) and 1.74 vs 0.75 GB/s (Apple A14, clang 12) against RapidJSON insitu. The author's own blog says the gap is small with GCC and large with MSVC and clang.
status_note: Stale: the last parser change was in September 2021 (a full int32 range fix), the 2025 commit only added Bazel support, and 8 issues plus 3 PRs are open. It is MIT-licensed and a single 2.6k-line header, so it is easy to vendor and patch.
